content.value: Every note in the series follows the same four-part structure to allow modular reading while building the series narrative:

items: Position — A declarative, falsifiable claim about vendor or market implication (PJA format: max 40 words)
Framework Evidence — The specific ASAF dimensions, sub-dimensions, principles, and maturity stage references that substantiate the position
Vendor Implications — Three buyer/vendor impact observations tied directly to the position
Actions — Three to five specific, non-obvious actions for the note's primary audience

content.value: CLUSTER: Anchor — reads as a standalone position paper and as the binding frame for all 11 subsequent notes. Published first; referenced last.

items: The Burning Platform: One crisp argument for why the tier model is ending — not 'AI is changing everything' but a specific falsifiable claim: enterprises at Stage 2 are eliminating L1/L2 workloads in production today. Name the buyer behavior, not the technology.

The Framework Map: The 6 stages, 3 operating planes, and 11 dimensions shown as a single conceptual diagram. Not explained in depth — oriented. The reader needs to understand the shape of the framework so every subsequent note has a home.

The Market Implication: The transition creates three vendor categories — those who enable stage advancement, those neutral to it, and those displaced by it. This note identifies which category is which and names the specific ASAF dimensions that drive each outcome.

The Series Navigation: A reader guide that tells people where to enter. 'If you build detection products, start with Notes 2–3. If you're a platform vendor, start with Note 5. If you're a CISO, start with Note 6.' Makes the series modular.

The Stakes Definition: The specific, datable claim that makes the position actionable — products built for Stage 0–1 operations are not being gradually deprecated; they are being architecturally substituted. The difference between gradual decline and substitution is the urgency.

content.value: CLUSTER A — Note 1 of 4. The conceptual bridge between the framework overview (Note 0) and the dimension-specific notes (Notes 2–4). It is the only note that explains why the three-plane model is the right architecture, not just what it is.

The three-plane model — Sensing, Reasoning, Control — is not an organizational chart; it is a signal processing architecture, and vendors who cannot identify which plane their product operates in cannot explain their role in an agentic security program.
Why This Note Exists Before Notes 2–4

Notes 2, 3, and 4 each cover one plane in depth (SEN, RSN, AGT). Without Note 1, a reader jumping into Note 2 understands what the Sensing dimension does but not why the plane architecture replaces the tier model. Note 1 makes the architectural argument once so Notes 2–4 can focus on vendor implications without re-explaining the theory.

content.value: CLUSTER A — Note 3 of 4. The Reasoning plane in depth. Primary audience: SIEM vendors, SOAR vendors, XDR platforms, investigation workflow products.

content.value: There is a structural difference between consuming from the SKG and writing to it. Products that only consume (read threat intelligence, query asset data) are replaceable by any other source of the same data. Products that write to the SKG — contributing unique adversary model updates, evidence artifacts, or confidence scores — accumulate a position that compounds over time. Every stage transition makes their contribution more valuable, not less.

content.value: CLUSTER B — Note 6 of 2. The highest-weight ASAF dimension (15%). Primary audience: GRC leaders, CISOs, CPOs, security product leaders building autonomous capabilities.

Security vendors that treat ethics and governance as policy documentation rather than operational runtime signals will be architecturally incompatible with Stage 3+ agentic SOC programs — enterprises building directed autonomy operations require machine-interpretable ethics guardrails, real-time authority enforcement, and unbreakable audit chains as first-class product capabilities, not compliance addendums.

GOV is weighted highest in the ASAF maturity model because it is the dimension with the most severe failure mode. A detection product that scores Stage 1 instead of Stage 2 produces less accurate alerts — a bounded, recoverable failure. A governance system that fails at Stage 3 exposes enterprises to legal liability for every ungoverned autonomous action — an unbounded, potentially irrecoverable failure. The weight reflects the asymmetry of consequences.

content.value: CAPSTONE — The final note in the series. Synthesizes all 11 dimensions into the operating cybernetic loop. Designed to be read after the full series AND independently by readers who want the complete system view before reading the individual notes.

The 11 ASAF dimensions are not independent capabilities — they form a continuous bidirectional signal loop where Sensing informs Reasoning, Reasoning directs Execution, Execution writes to the Knowledge Graph, the Knowledge Graph shapes Governance, and Governance constrains and recalibrates every other dimension; products that cannot participate in this loop are not evaluated as weaker competitors, they are excluded from the architecture before competitive evaluation begins.

content.value: Note 0 stated that the transition creates three vendor categories. Note 11 completes the argument: the categories are not based on product quality or feature breadth — they are based on integration depth in the cybernetic loop. A product with deep loop integration but narrow feature coverage is an Enabler. A product with broad feature coverage but shallow loop integration is Neutral at best. The loop is the architecture. Integration depth in the loop is the competitive moat.
